::: {.why}
Variance is not observed, so every evaluation compares a forecast against a noisy proxy, and the choice of loss function decides which model wins more often than the models differ.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- Say why mean squared error on squared returns is a defensible loss despite the proxy being extremely noisy, and what property makes QLIKE preferable.
- Show a case where two loss functions rank two volatility models differently.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>55 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Construct the disagreement: on your three models, find a sample period or a pair of models where mean squared error and QLIKE give opposite rankings, and explain it in terms of how each loss penalises under-prediction versus over-prediction.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Run the Mincer-Zarnowitz regression for each model, regressing realised variance on the forecast, and check whether the intercept is zero and the slope is one. A slope well below one means the forecast is too variable and should be shrunk, which is a fixable defect rather than a verdict.
:::
:::
